items.explanation: The passage says a degree is a signal, not a measure of learning, and employers use it to sort applicants, so students collect credentials rather than knowledge and the signal loses value as more people hold it. It does not claim degrees are worthless, that learning is impossible, or that employers ignore degrees.
options: A degree is a perfect measure of what a student has learned
A degree is worthless, because employers never look at it
Learning is impossible in a university, because all teaching is credentialism
A degree proves that a student is intelligent, regardless of what was studied
A degree is a signal employers use to sort applicants, so students collect credentials rather than knowledge, and the signal loses value as more people hold it
items.passage: Education is often described as the pursuit of knowledge, yet much of modern education is better described as the pursuit of credentials. A degree is not only, and sometimes not mainly, a record of what a student has learned. It is a signal, a way for an employer to sort a pile of applications quickly, to distinguish those who have passed a filter from those who have not. The signal works only as long as it is scarce. When everyone holds a degree, the degree alone no longer distinguishes anyone, and students must collect further credentials, a master's, a certificate, an internship, to stand out. The result is a race in which each generation must run further to reach the same place, spending more years and more money on signals that convey less information than they once did. This does not mean learning is worthless. It means the system rewards the appearance of learning more reliably than learning itself, and students, responding rationally to the incentives, optimise for grades and certificates rather than for understanding. A student who spends a term wrestling with a difficult idea may learn more than one who memorises the textbook, yet the second student will often receive the better grade. The remedy is not to abolish credentials, which serve a real purpose in sorting large numbers of applicants, but to separate the signal from the learning. Employers could test skills directly, universities could assess understanding rather than recall, and students could be judged by what they can do rather than by the certificates they hold. Until that separation happens, education will continue to produce graduates who are well credentialed and poorly educated, and the race for signals will continue to consume years that might have been spent learning. Employers contribute to the race when they raise degree requirements for jobs that do not need them, asking for a master's degree for work that could be learned in weeks. That practice, sometimes called credential inflation, forces applicants to spend years acquiring qualifications that add little to their ability to do the job, while excluding capable people who cannot afford the time or money. The employer gains a simple filter, and loses a wider pool of talent, yet the cost is borne by the applicant, not by the employer, so the practice continues. A fairer approach would be to test for the skills the job actually requires, and to value experience, portfolios and practical demonstrations as highly as certificates, so that the signal is tied to the work itself rather than to the length of time a person spent in a classroom.
items.question: What is the author's central claim about credentials in education?

items.explanation: The passage says students optimise for grades and certificates rather than understanding, so a student who memorises may get a better grade than one who wrestles with a difficult idea and learns more. That is the perverse incentive identified, not a claim that grades measure learning perfectly.
options: Grades always measure learning perfectly, so the best students always get the best grades
Students who wrestle with difficult ideas always receive the best grades
A student who memorises the textbook may receive a better grade than one who wrestles with a difficult idea and learns more, because the system rewards the appearance of learning
Memorisation is the best way to learn any subject deeply
Understanding is always rewarded more reliably than grades in the current system
items.question: What perverse incentive does the passage identify in the credential system?

items.explanation: The author proposes separating signal from learning: employers testing skills directly, universities assessing understanding rather than recall, and judging students by what they can do rather than certificates held. Abolishing credentials, collecting more of them, and judging only by certificates all contradict that proposal.
options: Abolish all credentials entirely, so that no one is ever sorted by a certificate
Separate the signal from the learning, by testing skills directly, assessing understanding rather than recall, and judging students by what they can do
Collect even more credentials, so that the signal becomes stronger as it becomes scarcer
Judge students only by the certificates they hold, ignoring what they can actually do
Spend more years and more money on signals, so that each generation runs further to reach the same place
items.question: What remedy does the author propose for credentialism?

items.explanation: The passage says a city can be crowded and lonely at once, because loneliness is not the absence of people but the absence of belonging, and urban life offers contact without connection. It is not about population size alone, rural life, or a lack of neighbours.
options: Loneliness is not the absence of people but the absence of belonging, so a crowded city can be lonely when contact does not become connection
Loneliness is caused only by living in a small village with few people
Loneliness disappears as soon as a city becomes more crowded
Loneliness is caused by having too many neighbours, not too few
Loneliness is a purely rural problem that does not affect cities
items.passage: A city can be crowded and lonely at the same time. Millions of people may live within a few square miles, sharing buses, lifts and pavements, yet never speak to one another, never learn a neighbour's name, never feel that they belong to the place where they live. Loneliness, in this account, is not the absence of people. It is the absence of belonging, the feeling that one is surrounded by strangers who will not notice if one disappears. Urban life is particularly good at producing this feeling, because it offers contact without connection. A person may interact with dozens of people in a day, a shopkeeper, a driver, a colleague, without any of those interactions becoming a relationship. The interactions are brief, transactional and replaceable, and they leave the person feeling more alone than if she had met no one at all. The remedy often proposed is more socialising, more events, more opportunities to meet people. Yet the problem is not a shortage of opportunities to meet strangers, but a shortage of structures that turn strangers into neighbours. A community is not a collection of individuals who happen to live near each other. It is a set of shared routines, obligations and stories, a market where the same faces return, a park where children play together, a building where people know who is ill and who needs help. Without those structures, a city is a collection of private lives lived in public, and loneliness, however crowded the streets, will persist. Housing design plays a part, because a building with no shared spaces, no courtyard and no place to linger will produce neighbours who never meet, however many people live in it. A building with a shared garden, a common room and a staircase wide enough for conversation will produce, over time, a community, not because its residents are friendlier but because its design gives them reasons to encounter each other. Urban planners who understand this design for encounter, placing benches where people wait, markets where they shop, and parks where children play, so that the city itself becomes a structure for belonging. A city built only for movement, for cars and for speed, will move people efficiently and leave them lonely, because it has designed out the very encounters that turn strangers into neighbours.
items.question: According to the passage, why can a crowded city be lonely?

items.explanation: The passage says interactions are brief, transactional and replaceable, and they leave a person feeling more alone than if she had met no one, because contact has not become connection. It does not claim urban people are unfriendly by nature or that cities have too few people.
options: Urban people are unfriendly by nature and refuse to speak to strangers
Cities have too few people, so residents rarely meet anyone at all
Urban interactions are long and deep, but they make people feel lonely anyway
Urban interactions are brief, transactional and replaceable, offering contact without connection, and can leave a person feeling more alone than meeting no one
Loneliness in cities is caused by a lack of shops, buses and lifts
items.question: How does urban life produce loneliness, according to the passage?

items.explanation: The author says the problem is not a shortage of opportunities to meet strangers but a shortage of structures that turn strangers into neighbours, such as shared routines, obligations and stories. More events alone, more people, and avoiding strangers all miss that point.
options: More social events and more opportunities to meet strangers, since the problem is a shortage of meetings
More people moving into the city, so that the streets become even more crowded
Avoiding strangers entirely, so that loneliness is not felt
Building more shops and buses, since infrastructure alone creates community
Creating structures that turn strangers into neighbours, such as shared routines, obligations and stories
items.question: What does the author say is needed to reduce urban loneliness?

items.explanation: The passage says collective memory is the story a group tells about its past, shaped by what it chooses to remember and forget, and that forgetting is not accidental but a choice that shapes identity. It is not a perfect record, a purely individual matter, or a fixed fact.
options: Collective memory is a perfect record of everything that happened in the past
Collective memory is a purely individual matter, with no connection to group identity
Collective memory is the story a group tells about its past, shaped by what it chooses to remember and forget, and forgetting is a choice that shapes identity
Collective memory never changes, because the past is fixed and unchanging
Collective memory is identical to history, since both record the same facts in the same way
items.passage: History is often imagined as a record of what happened, but collective memory is something different. It is the story a group tells itself about its past, shaped as much by what it chooses to forget as by what it chooses to remember. A nation may remember its victories in detail and its crimes in vague outline, not because the crimes did not happen but because remembering them would disturb the story it tells about itself. Forgetting, in this account, is not an accident. It is a choice, made collectively and often unconsciously, to preserve a particular identity. The difficulty is that forgetting does not erase the past. It merely postpones the reckoning, and the past, unremembered, returns in other forms: in resentment, in distrust, in the repetition of old mistakes by people who do not know they are repeating them. A society that remembers honestly is not one that remembers everything, since no society can, but one that remembers the difficult parts as well as the proud ones, and that allows different groups within it to remember differently without accusing each other of disloyalty. Memory, in this sense, is not a luxury for historians. It is the material from which identity is made, and a society that cannot remember its own past cannot understand its present, or choose its future with any clarity. Museums and memorials are the places where this choice is made visible, because they decide which objects to display, which stories to tell, and which silences to preserve. A museum that displays only the triumphs of a nation tells a different story from one that displays its failures as well, and visitors who see only triumphs may leave with a pride that is unearned, while visitors who see failures may leave with a humility that is necessary. The best museums do not pretend to be neutral, because no display is neutral, but they are honest about their choices, labelling what is contested, presenting more than one perspective, and allowing visitors to form their own judgement. That honesty is itself a form of memory, a recognition that the past is not a single story but a set of stories that must be held together, even when they disagree.
items.question: What is the author's central claim about collective memory?

items.explanation: The passage says forgetting does not erase the past, it postpones the reckoning, and the past returns as resentment, distrust and repetition of old mistakes by people who do not know they are repeating them. It does not claim forgetting is harmless or that the past disappears.
options: Forgetting erases the past completely, so it can never return
Forgetting postpones the reckoning, and the unremembered past returns as resentment, distrust and repetition of old mistakes
Forgetting is always harmless, because the past has no effect on the present
Forgetting makes a society stronger, because it removes all difficult memories
Forgetting is an accident that no group ever chooses to do
items.question: What happens, according to the author, when a society forgets its difficult past?

items.explanation: The author says an honest society remembers difficult parts as well as proud ones and allows different groups to remember differently without accusing each other of disloyalty. Remembering everything, remembering only victories, and demanding a single memory all contradict that definition.
options: A society that remembers the difficult parts as well as the proud ones, and allows different groups to remember differently without accusing each other of disloyalty
A society that remembers everything that ever happened, in perfect detail
A society that remembers only its victories and forgets all its crimes
A society that demands every group remember the past in exactly the same way
A society that refuses to remember anything difficult, for the sake of unity
items.question: What does the author mean by a society that remembers honestly?

items.explanation: The passage says automation can make a worker faster while making the work less skilled, because the machine decides and the worker executes, so skill atrophies and the worker becomes replaceable. It is not about machines being slower, workers becoming more skilled, or technology having no effect.
options: Technology always makes workers more skilled, because it gives them more to learn
Technology has no effect on skill, because skill is fixed at birth
Technology makes workers slower, because machines are harder to use than human hands
Automation can make a worker faster while making the work less skilled, because the machine decides and the worker executes, so skill atrophies
Technology always creates more skilled jobs than it destroys, so deskilling never happens
items.passage: Technology is often praised for making work easier, yet ease can be a form of loss. When a machine takes over the skilled part of a job, the worker who remains may be faster, more productive and less skilled than before. A weaver who once chose threads, judged tension and repaired mistakes becomes an operator who presses a button when a light turns green. A driver who once navigated by memory and judgement becomes a follower of instructions from a screen. The work is done more quickly, but the worker knows less about how it is done, and that loss matters. Skill is not only a means to a wage. It is a source of pride, of identity, of the ability to judge whether work has been done well. A worker who has lost skill has also lost the capacity to notice when something is wrong, to improvise when the machine fails, and to teach the next generation what the work requires. The danger is not that machines will replace all workers, but that they will replace the skilled part of work, leaving workers who are dependent on systems they do not understand. A society that values only speed and output may not notice the loss until the machine breaks, and no one remembers how to do the work by hand. The remedy is not to reject technology, but to design it so that it augments skill rather than replacing it, keeping the human judgement at the centre of the work, even when the machine does the heavy lifting. Apprenticeship is the traditional answer to this problem, because it keeps the learner beside the skilled worker, watching, imitating and gradually taking on more of the task. The apprentice learns not only the movements but the judgements, when a thread is too tight, when a joint is weak, when a machine sounds wrong, and those judgements cannot be learned from a manual alone. Modern workplaces that replace apprenticeship with short training courses may produce workers who can operate a machine but cannot diagnose it, and the loss becomes visible only when the machine fails and no one knows why. Restoring apprenticeship, in new forms for new industries, would keep human judgement at the centre of work, and would ensure that skill is passed on, not merely used up, by each generation of workers.
items.question: What is the author's central claim about technology and deskilling?

items.explanation: The passage says skill is a source of pride, identity and the ability to judge whether work has been done well, and losing it removes the capacity to notice errors, improvise when the machine fails, and teach the next generation. It is not only about wages or speed.
options: Skill matters only because it determines how much a worker is paid
Skill matters only because it makes work faster
Skill matters only because it makes a worker harder to replace
Skill matters only in traditional crafts, not in modern work
Skill is a source of pride and identity, and of the ability to judge work, notice errors, improvise when a machine fails, and teach the next generation
items.question: Why does the loss of skill matter, according to the author?

items.explanation: The author says the remedy is not to reject technology but to design it so it augments skill rather than replacing it, keeping human judgement at the centre even when the machine does the heavy lifting. Rejecting technology, removing humans, and valuing only speed all contradict that remedy.
options: Reject all technology, so that no machine ever takes over skilled work
Remove human judgement entirely, so that machines decide everything
Design technology so that it augments skill rather than replacing it, keeping human judgement at the centre of the work
Value only speed and output, and ignore the loss of skill entirely
Ensure that no worker ever learns how to do work by hand, in case the machine breaks
items.question: What remedy does the author propose for deskilling?

items.explanation: The passage says punishment asks what the offender deserves while restorative justice asks what was harmed and what would repair it, bringing victim, offender and community together to agree on repair. It is not about abolishing all consequences, being lenient, or ignoring victims.
options: Punishment asks what the offender deserves, while restorative justice asks what was harmed and what would repair it, bringing victim, offender and community together to agree on repair
Punishment and restorative justice ask exactly the same question and differ only in name
Restorative justice means abolishing all consequences for offenders
Restorative justice is more lenient than punishment in every case, regardless of the harm
Restorative justice ignores victims entirely and focuses only on offenders
items.passage: Justice is usually imagined as punishment. A crime is committed, a penalty is imposed, and the balance is restored. Yet punishment, however necessary, answers only one question: what does the offender deserve? It does not ask what was harmed, what would repair the harm, or what the victim needs to feel safe again. Restorative justice begins with those questions. It brings victim, offender and community together, not to decide a penalty but to agree on a repair: an apology, restitution, community service, a change in behaviour. The offender is asked not only to suffer a consequence but to understand the harm and take responsibility for repairing it. Critics argue that restorative justice is soft, that it lets offenders off lightly and fails to deter others. There is force in the worry, and restorative justice is not appropriate for every crime. But the evidence, where it has been tried carefully, suggests that victims who participate often feel more satisfied than those who go through a conventional trial, and offenders who take part are less likely to reoffend than those who simply serve a sentence. The point is not to replace punishment entirely, but to recognise that punishment alone leaves the harm unrepaired. A society that punishes without repairing may feel that justice has been done, while the victim still lives with the loss and the offender still does not understand what was done. Justice, in this account, is not only about what the offender deserves. It is about what the community needs to heal, and that healing requires more than a penalty. Youth justice is a place where the restorative approach is often tried first, because young offenders are seen as capable of change, and because the harm they cause is often reparable. A teenager who has damaged property may be asked to repair it, to meet the owner, to understand the effect of the act, and to agree on a way to make amends. That process is slower than a fine or a short sentence, and it requires the victim to be willing to participate, yet when it works, it produces something a penalty cannot, which is an offender who understands what was done and a victim who feels heard. The approach is not suitable for every case, and it should not be romanticised, but its success with young people suggests that the questions it asks, what was harmed and what would repair it, are questions that justice should ask more often, for offenders of every age.
items.question: What is the author's central distinction between punishment and restorative justice?

items.explanation: The passage says victims who participate often feel more satisfied than those in a conventional trial, and offenders who take part are less likely to reoffend than those who simply serve a sentence. It does not claim restorative justice is appropriate for every crime or that it always lets offenders off lightly.
options: Restorative justice is appropriate for every crime, without exception
Victims who participate often feel more satisfied than those in a conventional trial, and participating offenders are less likely to reoffend than those who simply serve a sentence
Restorative justice always lets offenders off lightly and never deters anyone
Victims who participate always feel less satisfied than those in a conventional trial
Offenders who take part in restorative justice are more likely to reoffend than those who serve a sentence
items.question: What evidence does the author cite for restorative justice?

items.explanation: The author says the point is not to replace punishment entirely but to recognise punishment alone leaves harm unrepaired, and justice is about what the community needs to heal, which requires more than a penalty. Abolishing punishment and ignoring victims both contradict that conclusion.
options: Punishment should be abolished entirely, because it never works at all
Punishment alone is sufficient, because it always repairs the harm done
Restorative justice should ignore victims and focus only on offenders
Punishment alone leaves harm unrepaired, so justice must also address what the community needs to heal, which requires more than a penalty
Justice is only about what the offender deserves, and nothing else matters
items.question: Which conclusion does the author draw about justice?

items.explanation: The poem shows the train carrying people who do not know each other, each with a ticket, a suitcase and a story, and the speaker learning that a journey is not only about arrival but about the brief, shared silence between strangers. The other readings ignore the shared carriage or invent a complaint about trains.
options: The speaker hates travelling by train and wishes to go by car instead
The speaker believes trains are always late and unreliable
The train carries strangers who share a brief, silent journey, and the speaker learns that a journey is about the shared silence between strangers as well as arrival
The speaker is angry at the other passengers for talking too loudly
The speaker believes that a ticket is more important than the journey itself
items.passage: The night train left at ten, with a sigh, / and carried us through fields we could not see, / past towns with names we could not pronounce, / past rivers that ran black beneath the moon. // In our carriage, no one spoke at first, / each with a ticket, a suitcase, a story, / a woman with a child who would not sleep, / a man with a letter he kept reading, and reading. // At midnight, the train stopped at a station, / and a vendor called out tea, tea, hot tea, / and for a moment, we were not strangers, / but travellers, sharing a cup, sharing the night. // By dawn, we had arrived, and parted, / without names, without addresses, without goodbye, / and I understood, as the train pulled away, / that a journey is not only about arrival, / but about the brief, shared silence / between strangers, on a train, in the night.
items.question: What does the night train journey chiefly suggest in the poem?

items.explanation: The vendor's call and the shared cup turn strangers into travellers for a moment, showing that a small, ordinary act can create a brief community among people who otherwise do not speak. It is not a complaint about tea, a delay, or a sign the train has broken down.
options: A small, ordinary act, sharing tea, can briefly turn strangers into fellow travellers, creating a moment of community
The vendor is trying to sell tea for an unfair price and should be ignored
The train has broken down and the passengers are waiting for help
The passengers are angry at the vendor for waking them up
Tea is the only reason anyone travels by train at night
items.question: The image of sharing tea at midnight most nearly suggests that

items.explanation: The argument assumes reading itself causes the better vocabulary rather than other differences between readers and non-readers explaining both. The other options are stronger claims the argument does not need, such as every reader having a better vocabulary or reading being the only cause.
options: Every person who reads regularly has a better vocabulary than every person who does not
Reading is the only cause of a good vocabulary in any population
People who do not read never learn new words at all
Reading itself causes the better vocabulary, rather than other differences between readers and non-readers
Reading is more important than speaking, listening and writing combined
items.question: A survey finds people who read regularly have a better vocabulary than people who do not. A writer concludes that reading improves vocabulary. Which assumption is required?

items.explanation: If the new park also opened a free gym at the same time, the gym is an alternative cause for the rise in exercise, weakening the claim that the park alone caused it. Residents liking the park, the park being popular, and the mayor's experience are weaker or irrelevant.
options: Some residents said they liked the new park
The new park also opened a free gym at the same time, offering an alternative cause for the rise in exercise
Exercise also rose slightly in a neighbourhood without a new park
The park was popular with younger residents in particular
The mayor had ten years of experience in urban planning
items.question: A town builds a new park and finds that residents exercise more in the following year. The mayor argues the park caused the rise. Which finding most weakens the argument?

items.explanation: Because the coffee drinkers also differ in age and work hours, those differences could explain the alertness gap, so the study cannot establish that coffee alone caused it. It does not prove coffee has no effect, nor that non-drinkers will always be less alert.
options: Drinking coffee alone causes greater alertness, regardless of age or work hours
Coffee has no effect on alertness at all
People who do not drink coffee will always be less alert
Age and work hours are irrelevant to alertness
The study cannot establish that coffee alone caused the difference, because the groups also differed in age and work hours
items.question: A study finds people who drink coffee in the morning are more alert than those who do not. However, the coffee drinkers are younger on average and work longer hours. Which conclusion is best supported?

items.explanation: Lugubrious means mournful or gloomy, especially in appearance, so mournful is closest. Cheerful and joyful are opposites, lively concerns energy rather than gloom, and loud concerns volume rather than sorrow.
options: Cheerful
Joyful
Mournful
Lively
Loud
items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to LUGUBRIOUS.

items.explanation: Neither nor takes the nearer subject, the players, so were is correct, while the other options mismatch singular and plural subjects. The number takes has, each takes was, and neither the coach nor the players takes were in the distractor with was.
options: Neither the coach nor the players were present at practice.
Neither the coach nor the players was present at practice.
The number of players have increased this year.
Each of the players are present today.
The team, along with the captain, are travelling tomorrow.
items.question: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

items.explanation: The order must open with the old school, then its silence, then the teacher's decision, then the return of children, then the lesson, giving B, A, D, C, E. Starting with E states the lesson first, and C before D returns children before the teacher opens the door.
options: B, D, A, C, E
A, B, D, C, E
D, B, A, C, E
B, A, D, C, E
E, B, A, D, C
items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The classrooms stood empty and silent, and the teacher wondered if anyone would ever return. (B) The old school on the hill had survived fire, flood and a change of government. (C) Within a year, the school was full again, not because the books had changed but because the door had been opened. (D) She began to leave the door open at dawn, to put a chair outside, and to greet every child by name. (E) A school, she learned, is not a building of books but a habit of welcome. Choose the correct order.

items.explanation: The sequence runs from the gardener planting, to the drought, to the well running dry, to the neighbours sharing water, to the lesson that a garden is a well, giving A, B, C, D, E. Any opening other than A puts an effect before its cause, and E before D states the lesson before the sharing that proves it.
options: A, C, B, D, E
A, B, C, D, E
E, A, B, C, D
A, B, D, C, E
B, A, C, D, E
items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The gardener planted his garden in March, as his mother had done before him. (B) The drought came in April, and the sky stayed empty for weeks. (C) By June, the well had run dry, and the garden was dust. (D) The neighbours shared their water, a little each day, until the rains returned. (E) A garden, the gardener learned, is not a place but a well that is shared. Choose the correct order.

items.explanation: The sentence needs a word for brief and a word for lasting: ephemeral for the attention and perennial for the dispute fits, while the other pairs mix a long word with a short word in the wrong order or pair two long words. Transient is close but ephemeral is the precise counterpart to perennial here.
options: perennial and transient
transient and perennial
transient and enduring
perennial and ephemeral
ephemeral and perennial
items.question: Fill in the blanks with the most appropriate pair. The media attention is _______, lasting barely a week, while the border dispute itself is _______, having survived three generations. (1) ephemeral (2) perennial (3) transient (4) enduring

items.explanation: A man holding an umbrella labelled Hope over a small seedling labelled Tomorrow, while rain labelled Doubt falls around him, shows that hope protects fragile future possibilities from doubt, even when doubt is widespread. The literal readings miss the labels, and the umbrella being useless or the rain being helpful are not the point.
options: Hope protects fragile future possibilities from doubt, even when doubt is widespread and the future is still small
Umbrellas are useless in the rain and should not be used
Doubt is helpful for seedlings and should be encouraged
The man should stop protecting the seedling and let the rain fall on it
Seedlings do not need protection from rain at all
items.question: The cartoon shows a man holding a small umbrella labelled Hope over a tiny seedling labelled Tomorrow, while heavy rain labelled Doubt falls all around him. The man is smiling, and the seedling is still standing. What message does the cartoon most likely convey?

items.explanation: If the supplier has falsified quality records before, the firm cannot trust the supplier's assurance that this batch is safe, which makes the case for recall decisive. The supplier being the cheapest and the firm having no alternative explain the dependence but do not make the batch safe. A rival using the same supplier does not change the facts. The drug being for a common illness raises the stakes but does not prove the batch is faulty.
options: The supplier is the cheapest source of the ingredient in the country
The firm has no alternative supplier for this ingredient
A rival firm also buys the same ingredient from this supplier
The drug is used to treat a common illness
The supplier has falsified quality records for this ingredient in the past
items.passage: A pharmaceutical firm has discovered that a key ingredient supplied for its best-selling blood pressure drug may be contaminated, after a routine test showed an impurity above the permitted limit. The firm has already distributed 20 lakh packs of the drug to pharmacies across the country, and the supplier, which provides 80 percent of the firm's supply of this ingredient, says the test result was a laboratory error and that the ingredient is safe. The firm's own quality head wants an immediate recall of all packs made with the suspect ingredient, arguing that a contaminated blood pressure drug could harm patients who depend on it daily. The commercial head warns that a recall would cost 15 crore rupees, would create a shortage of the drug for patients who need it, and would damage the firm's reputation with doctors. The regulatory affairs head notes that the regulator must be informed within 48 hours if the firm has reason to believe a drug is unsafe, and that hiding the result could lead to a factory closure. The chief executive must decide today, because the next batch of the drug is due to leave the factory tomorrow morning. The pharmacies have already sold most of the 20 lakh packs to patients who take the drug every day for blood pressure. The doctors who prescribe the drug have asked the firm whether the packs they prescribed are safe, and the firm has not yet answered them. The next batch of the drug is due to leave the factory tomorrow morning, and the production team is waiting for the chief executive's decision. The supplier provides 80 percent of the firm's supply of this ingredient and has no alternative source in the country.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support recalling the drug immediately?

items.explanation: A recall with a published batch list, a helpline and an alternative supply arrangement protects patients and gives doctors a clear action, while the regulator is informed on time. Waiting for proof of harm leaves patients exposed. Quietly withdrawing from pharmacies does not reach patients who already hold packs. Blaming the supplier publicly does not protect patients. Continuing to sell while testing repeats the risk.
options: Recall all packs made with the suspect ingredient, publish the batch numbers, set up a helpline, inform the regulator within the deadline, and arrange an alternative supply for patients
Wait for reports of patient harm before taking any action
Quietly withdraw packs from pharmacies without telling patients or the regulator
Blame the supplier in a press release and continue selling the drug
Continue selling the drug while the test is repeated in another laboratory
items.question: What should the chief executive do today?

items.explanation: If the impurity is harmless at the level found and breaks down before reaching patients, the quality head's fear of harm is overstated, which weakens the case for a costly recall. A past falsification and a regulator deadline both support recall. The cost of a recall is a reason to hesitate but does not show the drug is safe. A rival using the same supplier does not prove this batch is safe.
options: The supplier has falsified quality records in the past
Independent tests show the impurity is harmless at the level found and breaks down before the drug reaches patients
The regulator must be informed within 48 hours if the drug may be unsafe
A recall would cost 15 crore rupees
A rival firm also buys the same ingredient from this supplier
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the quality head's argument for an immediate recall?

items.explanation: If buyers rank the service network above price, the firm's dealer network is a genuine advantage that a price war would waste, while matching the rival price destroys the margin that funds that network. A rival raising prices later does not justify a cut now. A new model next year does not solve this year's sales. Cheaper batteries alone do not justify matching the rival. A government subsidy for buyers is a market fact, not a reason to hold price.
options: The rival plans to raise its prices after the festive season
A new model with a longer range will be ready next year
A survey shows that most buyers of electric two-wheelers rank the service network and spare parts availability above a lower price
The firm has found a cheaper battery supplier for next year
The government offers a subsidy to buyers of electric two-wheelers
items.passage: A maker of electric two-wheelers has seen its sales fall by 30 percent in six months after a new rival launched a similar vehicle at 25 percent below its price. The rival vehicle has a shorter range and a smaller service network, but its low price has attracted first-time buyers who have never owned an electric vehicle. The firm's own vehicle has a longer range, a network of 200 service centres, and a five-year battery warranty, while the rival offers only a two-year warranty and 40 service centres. The sales head wants to cut the price by 20 percent to match the rival, arguing that first-time buyers care only about price and that market share is being lost every week. The finance head warns that a 20 percent cut would make every vehicle loss-making, and that the firm would run out of cash within a year at that price. The product head argues that the firm should instead improve its financing offers and its service network, and let the rival's buyers discover the cost of poor service. The chief executive must decide before the festive season, when two-wheeler sales double and the rival is planning a large advertising campaign. The festive season starts in eight weeks, when two-wheeler sales double and the rival is planning a large advertising campaign. The firm's dealers have asked for bigger discounts to match the rival's price, and two dealers have said they will switch to the rival if the firm does not act. The finance head has calculated that a 20 percent price cut would make every vehicle loss-making and that the firm would run out of cash within a year. The product head has proposed better financing offers and a stronger service network instead.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support holding the price instead of matching the rival?

items.explanation: If rival buyers return within a year because of service failures, the rival's low price is a short-term gain that turns into a loss, which strengthens the case for holding price and letting the rival's weakness show. A new advertising campaign and a cheaper battery are pressures, not evidence. First-time buyers caring only about price supports cutting. A dealer asking for a discount is a negotiation point, not proof.
options: The rival is planning a large advertising campaign for the festive season
The rival has found a cheaper battery supplier
First-time buyers say they care only about the purchase price
Most buyers who chose the rival in the last year have returned to established brands within a year because of service failures and battery problems
A large dealer has asked the firm for a bigger discount to match the rival
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support the product head's view that the firm should hold its price and invest in service?

items.explanation: Cutting the price to a loss-making level is a financial fact against the cut, not a reason to make it, so it is the exception. The rival's shorter range, the firm's service network, the five-year warranty, and the risk of running out of cash are all genuine reasons to hold the price.
options: The rival vehicle has a shorter range than the firm's vehicle
The firm has 200 service centres against the rival's 40
The firm offers a five-year battery warranty against the rival's two years
The firm's service network is the largest in its segment
A 20 percent price cut would make every vehicle loss-making
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to hold the price instead of matching the rival EXCEPT

items.explanation: If the mine's water use has already lowered the water table and wells are running dry, the harm to the village is concrete and current, which makes the case for limiting the mine's water use decisive. The mine paying taxes and employing villagers are benefits, not reasons to ignore the water harm. A new borewell for the village would be a remedy, not a reason to continue. The mine being the largest employer explains the pressure but does not excuse the harm.
options: The mine's water use has already lowered the water table and village wells are running dry
The mine pays a large share of the district's tax revenue
The mine employs 400 people from the surrounding villages
The mine has offered to dig a new borewell for the village
The mine is the largest employer in the district
items.passage: A mining company operates an iron ore mine that employs 400 people and pays a large share of the district's tax revenue. The mine uses large amounts of groundwater, and the water table in the surrounding villages has fallen sharply in the last three years. Village wells are running dry, farmers say their crops have failed for two seasons, and women now walk four kilometres to fetch water. The company argues that it holds a valid mining licence, that it pays compensation to affected families, and that closing or limiting the mine would leave 400 families without income. The village council has asked the district officer to limit the mine's water use and to require the company to supply water to the villages until the water table recovers. The company offers to dig a new borewell for the village and to pay for water tankers for six months, but refuses to limit its own water use, arguing that its production targets depend on it. The district officer must decide before the summer, when the water shortage will be at its worst and the village council has threatened a protest that would block the road to the mine. The summer starts in two months, when the water shortage will be at its worst and the village council has threatened a protest that would block the road to the mine. The farmers say their crops have failed for two seasons and women now walk four kilometres to fetch water. The company has offered to dig a new borewell and to pay for water tankers for six months, but it refuses to limit its own water use. The district officer must decide before the summer, and the mine's licence is due for renewal next year.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support limiting the mine's water use?
items.set_title: DM3: The Mine and the Village Wells

items.explanation: Limiting the mine's water use to a sustainable level, supplying water to the villages until the water table recovers, and publishing the water data addresses the harm at its source while keeping the mine open. Accepting the borewell alone leaves the mine's use unchecked. Closing the mine at once destroys 400 jobs without a transition. Ignoring the council invites a protest that blocks the road. Paying compensation alone does not restore the water.
options: Accept the company's offer of a borewell and water tankers for six months and impose no limit on the mine's water use
Limit the mine's water use to a sustainable level set by an independent study, require the company to supply water to the villages until the water table recovers, and publish monthly water data
Close the mine immediately without any transition plan for the 400 workers
Ignore the village council and let the company continue as before
Pay higher compensation to affected families and change nothing else
items.question: What should the district officer do?
items.set_title: DM3: The Mine and the Village Wells

items.explanation: If the company has already breached its licence conditions on water use twice, its promise to comply in future is not credible, which weakens the case for trusting its voluntary offer. The mine employing villagers and paying taxes are benefits, not evidence of compliance. A protest blocking the road is a pressure, not proof. The summer shortage being worst is a reason to act, not a reason to trust the company.
options: The mine employs 400 people from the surrounding villages
The mine pays a large share of the district's tax revenue
The company has already breached its licence conditions on water use twice in the last three years
The village council has threatened a protest that would block the road to the mine
The water shortage will be at its worst in the summer
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the company's argument that its voluntary offer is enough?
items.set_title: DM3: The Mine and the Village Wells

items.explanation: If the chief executive has already told the board about the illness and asked for a succession plan, the information is not a secret the human resources head must protect, which supports discussing it openly with the board. The illness being private is a reason for care, not a reason to hide a succession risk. A rival learning of it is a risk to manage. The head's friendship with the chief executive is a conflict, not a justification. The board meeting being next week is a deadline, not evidence.
options: The illness is a private medical matter and the chief executive has asked for confidentiality
A rival firm could use the news to poach the company's clients
The human resources head is a close friend of the chief executive
The chief executive has already told the board about the illness and asked the head to prepare a succession plan
The board meeting is next week and the succession item is on the agenda
items.passage: The human resources head of a listed company has learned from the chief executive's doctor, who is a personal friend, that the chief executive has a serious illness and may need to step down within six months. The chief executive has asked the human resources head to keep the information completely confidential, saying the chief executive will tell the board when the time is right. The human resources head knows that the board is about to approve a three-year strategy that depends on the chief executive leading it, that investors have been told the chief executive will stay for at least three years, and that the company has no succession plan. The head also knows that revealing the illness without the chief executive's consent would breach a personal confidence and could be seen as a betrayal. The head must decide whether to tell the board chair in confidence, to wait for the chief executive to disclose, or to raise the absence of a succession plan without mentioning the illness. The board meeting is in two weeks, and the strategy vote cannot be delayed without a public explanation. The board meeting is in two weeks and the strategy vote cannot be delayed without a public explanation to investors. The company has no succession plan and no deputy chief executive who could step in if the chief executive had to leave suddenly. Investors have been told the chief executive will stay for at least three years, and the three-year strategy depends on the chief executive leading it. The human resources head learned the information from the chief executive's doctor, who is a personal friend, and the chief executive has asked for complete confidentiality.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support telling the board chair in confidence?

items.explanation: If the company has no deputy who can step in, the absence of a succession plan is a live risk to the strategy the board is about to approve, which makes raising the issue urgent. The chief executive being popular and the strategy being important explain the stakes but do not show the risk. The doctor being a friend is the source of the conflict, not evidence. Investors being told the chief executive will stay is a consequence of the secrecy, not a reason to keep it.
options: The chief executive is popular with investors and employees
The three-year strategy is the most important decision the board will make this year
The doctor is a personal friend of the human resources head
Investors have been told the chief executive will stay for at least three years
The company has no deputy chief executive and no one who could step in if the chief executive had to leave suddenly
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support raising the absence of a succession plan with the board chair even without disclosing the illness?

items.explanation: Raising the succession gap with the chair in general terms, without disclosing the illness, protects confidentiality while giving the board a chance to prepare, which is the proportionate first step. Waiting silently leaves the board approving a strategy built on a person who may leave. Telling the full board at once breaches the confidence. Telling investors first is a disclosure the board should make, not the human resources head. Resigning avoids the decision rather than solving it.
options: Raise the absence of a succession plan with the board chair in general terms, without disclosing the illness, and ask the chair to insist on a plan before the strategy vote
Wait silently for the chief executive to disclose the illness
Tell the full board about the illness at the next meeting without the chief executive's consent
Inform investors before telling the board
Resign from the human resources role to avoid the decision
items.question: What should the human resources head do first?

items.explanation: Three experienced nurses resigning because of the surgeon's shouting shows the behaviour is already costing the hospital skilled staff, which is a concrete reason to act now. The surgeon's skill and the long waiting list explain why the director hesitates, but they do not make the behaviour acceptable. A rival offer is a risk, not evidence. A single apology last year does not undo a continuing pattern.
options: The surgeon is the most skilled in the hospital for complex operations
Three experienced nurses have resigned in the last six months, citing the surgeon's shouting and public humiliation of staff in the operating theatre
The waiting list for the surgeon's operations is six months long
A rival hospital has offered the surgeon a higher salary
The surgeon apologised once after a complaint last year
items.passage: A large hospital has a senior surgeon who performs complex operations that no other surgeon in the hospital can do, and whose patients have the best outcomes in the region. The same surgeon routinely shouts at nurses and junior doctors in the operating theatre, has thrown instruments on the floor twice, and has made two junior doctors cry in front of patients. Three experienced nurses have resigned in the last six months, citing the surgeon's behaviour, and the nursing head warns that more will leave. The hospital director fears that disciplining the surgeon could lead to the surgeon's resignation, which would leave complex cases with no one to treat them and would damage the hospital's reputation. The hospital has a written code of conduct that applies to all staff, and the medical council can suspend a doctor for repeated unprofessional behaviour. The director must decide before the next appraisal, when the surgeon expects the highest rating and a promotion to head of department, a role that would give the surgeon authority over the nurses who complained. The hospital director must decide before the next appraisal, when the surgeon expects the highest rating and a promotion to head of department. The nursing head has warned that more nurses will leave if the behaviour continues, and the hospital already struggles to recruit experienced theatre nurses. The medical council can suspend a doctor for repeated unprofessional behaviour, and the hospital's code of conduct applies to all staff regardless of skill. The surgeon's patients have the best outcomes in the region, which is why the director fears losing the surgeon.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support acting against the surgeon's behaviour now?

items.explanation: If the surgeon's outcomes are the same as other surgeons once case complexity is accounted for, the claim that the hospital cannot afford to lose the surgeon collapses, which weakens the director's fear. The nurses resigning and the medical council's power both support acting. The waiting list being long explains the fear but does not show the surgeon is irreplaceable. The surgeon apologising once does not address the pattern.
options: Three experienced nurses have resigned, citing the surgeon's behaviour
The medical council can suspend a doctor for repeated unprofessional behaviour
The surgeon's patient outcomes are the same as other surgeons in the hospital once the complexity of cases is taken into account
The waiting list for the surgeon's operations is six months long
The surgeon apologised once after a complaint last year
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the director's fear that disciplining the surgeon will leave complex cases untreated?

items.explanation: The surgeon's skill is a reason the director might hesitate, not a reason to act, so it is the exception. The resignations, the risk of a medical council suspension, the promotion putting the surgeon over the complainants, and the signal that skill excuses shouting are all genuine reasons to act now.
options: Three experienced nurses have resigned, citing the surgeon's behaviour
The medical council can suspend a doctor for repeated unprofessional behaviour
Promoting the surgeon would put the surgeon in authority over the nurses who complained
The surgeon is the most skilled in the hospital for complex operations
Ignoring the behaviour signals to staff that skill excuses shouting and humiliation
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to act against the surgeon's behaviour now EXCEPT

items.explanation: If the firm's own data shows that the automated system makes more errors on complex cases than the analysts do, the automation does not deliver the quality it promises, which strengthens the case for a slower, retrained transition. The system being cheaper and the rival using it are commercial pressures, not proof of quality. The analysts being older and the union warning are relevant but do not show the system fails. A new client is a gain, not evidence.
options: The automated system is cheaper to run than the analysts
A rival firm has already automated the same work
The analysts are mostly over 45 and would find new jobs difficult
The union has warned of a strike if any analyst is dismissed
The firm's own tests show the automated system makes more errors than the analysts on complex cases, which are the firm's most valuable work
items.passage: A financial services firm has bought an automated system that can do the routine work of 80 analysts, who check loan applications and prepare credit reports. The system is faster and cheaper, but it makes more errors on complex cases, and the firm has no plan for what happens to the analysts. The chief executive wants to dismiss all 80 analysts at once and rely on the system, arguing that the savings will fund growth and that the analysts can find other jobs. The operations head warns that the system's errors on complex cases could lead to bad loans, that the analysts hold knowledge about long-standing clients that the system does not have, and that dismissing 80 people at once will damage the firm's reputation and invite a strike. The human resources head proposes a phased transition over 18 months, with 40 analysts retrained to handle complex cases and to check the system's work, and 40 offered voluntary retirement with support to find new jobs. The board must decide before the next quarterly results, because the system licence must be renewed and the cost saving has already been promised to investors. The system licence must be renewed before the next quarterly results, and the cost saving from automation has already been promised to investors. The analysts hold knowledge about long-standing clients that the system does not have, and the operations head has warned that the system's errors on complex cases could lead to bad loans. The union has warned of a strike if any analyst is dismissed, and the human resources head has proposed retraining 40 analysts and offering the other 40 voluntary retirement with support.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support the phased transition over dismissing all 80 analysts at once?
items.set_title: DM6: The Analysts and the Machine

items.explanation: A phased transition with retraining for complex cases, a checking role for the system, and supported voluntary retirement protects quality and people while still delivering savings, which is the balanced path. Dismissing all 80 at once risks bad loans and a strike. Keeping all analysts unchanged wastes the investment. Dismissing only the oldest analysts is discriminatory. Waiting a year leaves the licence and the promised saving unresolved.
options: Adopt the phased transition over 18 months: retrain 40 analysts to handle complex cases and to check the system's work, and offer the other 40 voluntary retirement with support to find new jobs
Dismiss all 80 analysts at once and rely entirely on the automated system
Keep all 80 analysts and do not use the automated system at all
Dismiss only the 40 oldest analysts and keep the rest
Wait a year before deciding anything
items.question: What decision should the board take on the analysts and the automated system?
items.set_title: DM6: The Analysts and the Machine

items.explanation: If the complex cases handled by the analysts generate most of the firm's profit, losing the analysts' judgement on those cases would damage the business more than the savings gain, which weakens the case for full dismissal. The system being faster and the savings being promised to investors both support automation. The analysts being older is a hardship, not a commercial argument. The union warning is a risk of dismissal, not proof the system fails.
options: The automated system is faster than the analysts on routine cases
The complex cases handled by the analysts generate 60 percent of the firm's profit
The cost saving from automation has already been promised to investors
The analysts are mostly over 45 and would find new jobs difficult
The union has warned of a strike if any analyst is dismissed
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the chief executive's argument for dismissing all 80 analysts at once?
items.set_title: DM6: The Analysts and the Machine

items.explanation: If the billing errors affect mostly low-income prepaid users who cannot afford to lose money, the harm falls on the most vulnerable customers, which makes the case for immediate refunds decisive. The errors being caused by a software bug is a cause, not a justification. A rival having similar errors does not make this firm's errors acceptable. The regulator asking for a report is a process, not evidence of harm. The firm's revenue being large does not show the errors are small.
options: The billing errors were caused by a software bug introduced in the last update
A rival telecom firm has had similar billing errors
The billing errors affect mostly low-income prepaid users who cannot afford to lose money from their balance
The regulator has asked the firm for a report on the billing errors
The firm is the largest telecom operator in the country
items.passage: A telecom operator has discovered that a software bug has overcharged 8 lakh prepaid customers by small amounts, between 10 and 50 rupees each, over the last three months, totalling 12 crore rupees. The bug has been fixed, but the firm must decide whether to refund all affected customers automatically, to refund only those who complain, or to offer free data instead of cash. The customer service head wants automatic refunds to every affected customer, arguing that the money was taken without consent and that the firm's reputation depends on returning it. The finance head argues that automatic refunds would cost 12 crore rupees plus processing costs, that most customers have not noticed the small amounts, and that offering free data would cost the firm far less. The legal head warns that the regulator can impose a fine if the firm does not refund, and that a consumer group is preparing a complaint. The chief executive must decide this week, because the consumer group plans to go public with the story and the regulator has set a deadline for the firm's response. The consumer group plans to go public with the story this week and has already collected complaints from 10,000 customers. The regulator has set a deadline for the firm's response and can impose a fine if the firm does not refund the money. The finance head has said automatic refunds would cost 12 crore rupees plus processing costs, while free data would cost far less. The customer service head has argued that the firm's reputation depends on returning money that was taken without consent.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support automatic refunds to every affected customer?

items.explanation: Automatic refunds to every affected customer, with a published timetable and a regulator report, returns money taken without consent and is verifiable, while free data as an option preserves choice. Refunding only complainants leaves most victims uncompensated. Free data alone does not return the money. Doing nothing invites a fine. Blaming the software vendor does not help customers.
options: Refund only customers who complain about the overcharge
Offer free data instead of cash to all affected customers
Do nothing and hope most customers never notice
Refund every affected customer automatically to the same prepaid balance, publish the timetable, and report the progress to the regulator
Blame the software vendor publicly and take no further action
items.question: Which announcement should the chief executive make this week?

items.explanation: Free data as an option is a benefit to customers who choose it, not a criticism of the automatic refund plan, so it is the exception. The money being taken without consent, the regulator's power to fine, the consumer group's complaint, the vulnerability of low-income users, and the reputational damage from silence are all genuine reasons to refund automatically.
options: The money was taken from customers without their consent
Free data would be popular with some customers who use a lot of data
The regulator can impose a fine if the firm does not refund the money
A consumer group is preparing a public complaint about the overcharge
The errors affect mostly low-income prepaid users who cannot afford the loss
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to refund every affected customer automatically EXCEPT
A merchant buys a bag for Rs 1000, marks it 70% above the cost price and sells it at a discount of 20% on the marked price. What is his profit percentage?
items.explanation: The marked price is Rs 1000 x 1.70 = Rs 1700. The selling price after the 20% discount is Rs 1700 x 0.80 = Rs 1360, so the profit is Rs 360 on a cost of Rs 1000, which is 36%. The other options come from applying the discount to the cost price or from adding the two percentages.

items.question: Two trains start from stations 500 km apart and move towards each other at 120 km/h and 80 km/h. How far from the first train's starting station do they meet?
options: 200 km
250 km
300 km
350 km
400 km
items.explanation: The trains close at 200 km/h, so they meet after 500/200 = 2.5 hours. In that time the first train covers 120 x 2.5 = 300 km. The meeting point is not the midpoint, since the first train is faster, and the distance from the second station is 200 km.

items.question: A sum of Rs 180 is divided between two people in the ratio 5:4. How much does the person with the larger share receive?
options: Rs 80
Rs 90
Rs 120
Rs 100
Rs 60
items.explanation: The larger share is 5/9 of Rs 180, which is Rs 180 x 5/9 = Rs 100. The smaller share is Rs 80. Dividing the sum equally, or using the ratio the wrong way round, gives the other options.

items.question: Five batsmen score distinct positive integer numbers of runs, and their average is 28 runs. What is the maximum possible value of the largest run?
items.explanation: The sum of all 5 values is 5 x 28 = 140. To make the largest value as big as possible, the other 4 values must be as small as possible while staying distinct and positive, so they are 1, 2, 3, 4, summing to 10. The largest value is therefore 140 - 10 = 130. Forgetting that the values must be distinct, or using the average itself as the maximum, gives the wrong options.

items.question: 12 men can finish a job in 10 days. After working for 4 days, 4 men leave. In how many more days will the remaining men finish the job?
options: 6 days
12 days
9 days
8 days
10 days
items.explanation: The job needs 120 man-days. In 4 days the 12 men complete 48 man-days, leaving 72 man-days. The remaining 8 men need 72/8 = 9 more days. Counting the 4 days already worked as part of the remaining time, or using 12 men throughout, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A sector of a circle of radius 14 cm has a central angle of 90 degrees. What is the area of the sector? (Use pi = 22/7)
options: 308 sq cm
77 sq cm
616 sq cm
200 sq cm
154 sq cm
items.explanation: The sector is one quarter of the full circle, so its area is (1/4) x (22/7) x 14 squared = (1/4) x 616 = 154 sq cm. Using the full circle area, or half of it, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the area of the largest square that can be inscribed in a circle of radius 8 cm?
options: 64 sq cm
256 sq cm
128 sq cm
100 sq cm
200 sq cm
items.explanation: The diagonal of the largest inscribed square is the diameter, 16 cm. Its area is half the square of the diagonal, (16 squared)/2 = 128 sq cm. Equivalently the area is 2R squared = 2 x 64 = 128 sq cm. Using the radius as the side gives the wrong options.

items.question: A triangle has a base of 20 cm and a height of 12 cm. What is its area?
options: 120 sq cm
240 sq cm
160 sq cm
100 sq cm
90 sq cm
items.explanation: The area is half the base times the height, (1/2) x 20 x 12 = 120 sq cm. Forgetting the half, or adding the base and height, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A square is inscribed in a right-angled triangle with legs 12 cm and 16 cm, with one corner at the right angle and the opposite corner on the hypotenuse. What is the side of the square?
options: 6 cm
7 cm
8 cm
5 cm
items.explanation: For a square of side s in a right triangle with legs a and b, 1/s = 1/a + 1/b, so s = ab/(a+b) = (12 x 16)/(12+16) = 192/28 = 48/7 cm. Half of either leg, or the average of the legs, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the curved surface area of a hemisphere of radius 14 cm? (Use pi = 22/7)
options: 616 sq cm
1848 sq cm
924 sq cm
1500 sq cm
1232 sq cm
items.explanation: The curved surface area of a hemisphere is 2 x pi x r squared = 2 x (22/7) x 196 = 1232 sq cm. The full surface area, which adds the circular base, is larger, and the area of a full sphere is a different value again.

items.question: What is the units digit of 7 raised to the power 2026?
items.explanation: The units digits of powers of 7 cycle as 7, 9, 3, 1 with period 4. Since 2026 leaves remainder 2 on division by 4, the units digit is the 2th term of the cycle, which is 9. The base 7 itself and the other cycle values are the distractors.

items.question: The HCF of two numbers is 12 and their LCM is 360. If one of the numbers is 72, what is the other number?
items.explanation: For any two numbers, their product equals HCF x LCM, so the other number is 12 x 360 / 72 = 4320/72 = 60. The LCM itself, or the HCF, or the difference of the two given numbers, gives the wrong options.

items.question: How many divisors of 720 are perfect squares?
items.explanation: Factorising, 720 = 2 to the power 4 x 3 squared x 5. A divisor is a perfect square exactly when every exponent is even, so the exponent of 2 can be 0, 2 or 4 (3 choices), of 3 can be 0 or 2 (2 choices), and of 5 can only be 0 (1 choice). The count is 3 x 2 x 1 = 6. Counting all divisors, or only the squares up to 720, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the minimum positive number that must be added to 1234 to make it divisible by 11?
items.explanation: 1234 leaves remainder 2 on division by 11, since 11 x 112 = 1232. To reach the next multiple of 11, 1243, we must add 11 - 2 = 9. Adding the remainder itself, or the quotient, gives the wrong options.

items.question: If x = 2 + sqrt(3), what is the value of x + 1/x?
items.explanation: Here 1/x = 1/(2 + sqrt(3)) = 2 - sqrt(3) after rationalising. So x + 1/x = (2 + sqrt(3)) + (2 - sqrt(3)) = 4. The square roots cancel exactly, and any option that keeps a sqrt(3) term is wrong.

items.question: What is the minimum value of (x - 2) squared + (x - 5) squared, where x is a real number?
items.explanation: Expanding gives 2x squared - 14x + 29 = 2(x - 7/2) squared + 9/2. The squared term is never negative, so the minimum is 9/2, attained at x = 7/2. The value at x = 2 or x = 5 is 9, which is larger, and the sum of the two constants is a distractor.

items.question: Three fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is 10?
items.explanation: There are 6 cubed = 216 equally likely outcomes, and 27 of them sum to 10, so the probability is 27/216 = 1/8. Counting only the ordered triples with distinct faces, or using the number of partitions of 10, gives the wrong options.

items.question: A committee of 4 is to be chosen from 6 men and 5 women. In how many ways can it be chosen if it must contain at least 2 women?
items.explanation: Count by the number of women: 2 women and 2 men gives C(5,2) x C(6,2) = 150 ways; 3 women and 1 man gives C(5,3) x C(6,1) = 60 ways; 4 women gives C(5,4) = 5 ways. The total is 150 + 60 + 5 = 215. Choosing any 4 from 11, or requiring exactly 2 women, gives the wrong options.

items.question: Is the integer n even? Statement I: n squared is even. Statement II: n is a multiple of 3.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Either statement alone is sufficient.
Neither statement alone nor both together are sufficient.
items.explanation: If n squared is even then n itself must be even, since the square of an odd number is odd, so statement I alone is sufficient. Statement II alone does not settle it, because multiples of 3 include both even numbers like 6 and odd numbers like 9. Hence statement I alone is sufficient.

items.question: What is the total budget allocation across all departments in 2025?

diagram.caption: Budget allocation (Rs crore) by department, 2024 and 2025

options: Rs 950 crore
Rs 1000 crore
Rs 925 crore
Rs 1025 crore
Rs 975 crore
items.explanation: Adding the 2025 column gives 150 + 220 + 90 + 340 + 175 = Rs 975 crore. The 2024 total is 850 crore, which is a distractor.

items.question: Which department recorded the largest absolute increase in budget from 2024 to 2025?
options: R&D
Operations
Marketing
HR
IT
items.explanation: The increases are R&D Rs 30 crore, Marketing Rs 20 crore, HR Rs 10 crore, Operations Rs 40 crore and IT Rs 25 crore, so Operations increased the most. R&D has the highest percentage increase, but the question asks for the absolute increase.

items.question: What is the percentage increase in the R&D budget from 2024 to 2025?
items.explanation: The R&D budget rose from Rs 120 crore to Rs 150 crore, an increase of Rs 30 crore on Rs 120 crore, which is 25%. Computing the increase on the 2025 base gives the wrong options.

items.question: How much does the household spend on food per month?

diagram.caption: Monthly household expenditure shares (%), total income Rs 80,000

items.explanation: Food is 35% of Rs 80000, which is Rs 28000. The other shares give the wrong options.

items.question: How much does the household spend on rent and transport together per month?
items.explanation: Rent is 25% and transport is 15%, together 40% of Rs 80000, which is Rs 32000. Adding only one of the two shares gives the wrong options.

items.question: By how much does the monthly spending on food exceed the monthly savings?
items.explanation: Food is 35% and savings is 10%, a gap of 25 percentage points, which is 25% of Rs 80000 = Rs 20000. The gap between food and rent is smaller and is a distractor.

items.question: How many patients recovered in total across the three wards?

diagram.caption: Patients and recovery rates in three hospital wards
diagram.content: A hospital has three wards. The General ward has 200 patients with a recovery rate of 85%. The ICU has 80 patients with a recovery rate of 60%. The Paediatric ward has 120 patients with a recovery rate of 90%.

options: 300 patients
352 patients
312 patients
340 patients
326 patients
items.explanation: Recovered patients are General: 170, ICU: 48 and Paediatric: 108, totalling 326. The total number of patients is 400, which is a distractor.

items.question: Which ward has the lowest recovery rate?
options: ICU
General
Paediatric
General and Paediatric together
All three are equal
items.explanation: The recovery rates are General 85%, ICU 60% and Paediatric 90%, so ICU has the lowest rate. The ICU also has the fewest patients, but the question asks for the rate, not the count.

items.question: What is the overall recovery percentage across all three wards?
items.explanation: 326 of the 400 patients recovered, so the overall recovery rate is 326/400 x 100 = 81.5%. Averaging the three ward rates gives 78.33%, which is wrong because the wards have different sizes.

items.question: Who won the men's singles title at the French Open in 2025?
options: Carlos Alcaraz
Jannik Sinner
Novak Djokovic
Alexander Zverev
Lorenzo Musetti
items.explanation: Carlos Alcaraz won the 2025 French Open men's singles title, beating Jannik Sinner in five sets in the longest French Open final ever played. Sinner finished runner-up, Djokovic lost in the semi-final, and Zverev and Musetti were eliminated earlier.

items.question: Which club won the FIFA Club World Cup in 2025?
options: Paris Saint-Germain
Chelsea
Real Madrid
Manchester City
Fluminense
items.explanation: Chelsea won the 2025 FIFA Club World Cup, beating Paris Saint-Germain 3-0 in the final in New Jersey in July 2025. Paris Saint-Germain finished runner-up, Real Madrid lost in the semi-final, and Manchester City and Fluminense did not reach the final.

items.question: Who became the Prime Minister of Canada in March 2025?
options: Justin Trudeau
Pierre Poilievre
Mark Carney
Jagmeet Singh
Chrystia Freeland
items.explanation: Mark Carney became Prime Minister of Canada in March 2025 after succeeding Justin Trudeau as leader of the Liberal Party. Trudeau resigned, Pierre Poilievre led the Conservative Party, Jagmeet Singh led the New Democratic Party, and Chrystia Freeland was a rival candidate in the Liberal leadership race.

items.question: The five-match Test series between India and England in 2025 ended with what result?
options: India won 3-2
England won 3-2
England won 4-1
The series was drawn 2-2
India won 4-1
items.explanation: The 2025 Test series between India and England ended in a 2-2 draw, with India winning the final Test at The Oval to level the series. Shubman Gill captained India in the series, and neither side won by 3-2 or 4-1.

items.question: The National Sports Governance Act, passed by Parliament in 2025, provides for which of the following?
options: A ban on foreign coaches
Government control of the BCCI
A national sports lottery
Compulsory sports in schools
A National Sports Board and a National Sports Tribunal
items.explanation: The National Sports Governance Act 2025 establishes a National Sports Board to recognise sports federations and a National Sports Tribunal to settle sports disputes. It does not ban foreign coaches, place the BCCI under government control, create a sports lottery, or make sports compulsory in schools.

items.question: Who was elected Mayor of New York City in November 2025?
options: Zohran Mamdani
Eric Adams
Andrew Cuomo
Curtis Sliwa
Brad Lander
items.explanation: Zohran Mamdani, the Democratic nominee, was elected Mayor of New York City in November 2025. Eric Adams was the incumbent who ran as an independent, Andrew Cuomo also ran as an independent, Curtis Sliwa was the Republican nominee, and Brad Lander lost the Democratic primary.

items.question: Who won the Tata Steel Chess Tournament (Masters) in 2025?
options: D. Gukesh
